items.title: 5.4 Condition of Concurrency of Three Straight Lines

source_refs.note: Book pp. 148-149: 5.4 Theorem 3 (condition of concurrency) with proof, Example 10 and a Challenge! box (missing sign corrected).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Three lines are called concurrent when all three pass through one common point, called the point of concurrency. Two non-parallel lines always meet at exactly one point, so for three lines the real question is: does the third line pass through the point where the first two meet? Theorem 3 turns this question into one number, a \(3 \times 3\) determinant made from the coefficients.

Three non-parallel lines
\[\ell_1 : a_1x + b_1y + c_1 = 0 \quad \ldots(i)\]
\[\ell_2 : a_2x + b_2y + c_2 = 0 \quad \ldots(ii)\]
\[\ell_3 : a_3x + b_3y + c_3 = 0 \quad \ldots(iii)\]
are concurrent iff
\[\begin{vmatrix} a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3 \end{vmatrix} = 0\]

blocks.latex: \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3 \end{vmatrix} = 0
blocks.text_alt: The determinant with rows a1 b1 c1, a2 b2 c2 and a3 b3 c3 equals zero

blocks.text:
If the lines are concurrent, then they have a common point of intersection \(P(x_1, y_1)\) say. As \(\ell_1 \nparallel \ell_2\), so their point of intersection \((x, y)\) is:
\[x = \dfrac{b_1c_2 - b_2c_1}{a_1b_2 - a_2b_1}\]
\[y = \dfrac{a_2c_1 - a_1c_2}{a_1b_2 - a_2b_1}\]
\((\because a_1b_2 - a_2b_1 \ne 0)\)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Where do these values of \(x\) and \(y\) come from? Solve (i) and (ii) together by Cramer's rule (or by elimination). The denominator \(a_1b_2 - a_2b_1\) is not zero exactly because \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) are not parallel: their slopes \(-\frac{a_1}{b_1}\) and \(-\frac{a_2}{b_2}\) are different. The book names the common point \(P(x_1, y_1)\) and then writes it as \((x, y)\); both names mean the same point.

This point also lies on (iii), so
\[a_3\left(\dfrac{b_1c_2 - b_2c_1}{a_1b_2 - a_2b_1}\right)\]
\[+ b_3\left(\dfrac{a_2c_1 - a_1c_2}{a_1b_2 - a_2b_1}\right) + c_3 = 0\]
or
\[a_3(b_1c_2 - b_2c_1)\]
\[+ b_3(a_2c_1 - a_1c_2)\]
\[+ c_3(a_1b_2 - a_2b_1) = 0\]
An easier way to write the above equation is in the following determinant form:
\[\begin{vmatrix} a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3 \end{vmatrix} = 0\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Step 1 to step 2: multiply the whole equation by \(a_1b_2 - a_2b_1\) (it is not zero), so the fractions disappear.
Step 2 to the determinant: expand the determinant along its third row. The cofactors of \(a_3\), \(b_3\), \(c_3\) are exactly \(b_1c_2 - b_2c_1\), \(a_2c_1 - a_1c_2\) and \(a_1b_2 - a_2b_1\), so the expansion gives the same equation.
This is necessary and sufficient condition iff of concurrency of given three lines.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints 'This is necessary and sufficient condition iff of concurrency of given three lines.' The word 'iff' is stray ('iff' already means 'necessary and sufficient'). It should read: 'This is the necessary and sufficient condition for the concurrency of the given three lines.'

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The proof above shows one direction: concurrent \(\Rightarrow\) determinant \(= 0\). The other direction also holds: if the determinant is \(0\) and \(\ell_1 \nparallel \ell_2\), read the steps backwards. The determinant equation is the last equation multiplied by \(a_1b_2 - a_2b_1 \ne 0\), so the meeting point of \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) satisfies (iii). That is why the condition is both necessary and sufficient. The words 'non-parallel' matter: three parallel lines also give a zero determinant, but they never meet.
Now the book applies Theorem 3 to three given lines.

blocks.title: Example 10
blocks.problem:
Check whether the following lines are concurrent or not. If concurrent, then find the point of concurrency.
\[3x - 2y - 2 = 0\]
\[x + y - 4 = 0\]
\[2x - y - 2 = 0\]
steps:
Given: \(3x - 2y - 2 = 0\), \(x + y - 4 = 0\), \(2x - y - 2 = 0\).
To find: whether they are concurrent, and if so the point of concurrency.
Method: Theorem 3. Put the coefficients \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) of each line in a row and evaluate the determinant. If it is \(0\), the lines are concurrent; then the meeting point of any two of them is the point of concurrency.

Write the determinant of the coefficients
\[\begin{vmatrix} 3 & -2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & -4 \\ 2 & -1 & -2 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: row 1 is \(3, -2, -2\) from the first line, row 2 is \(1, 1, -4\), row 3 is \(2, -1, -2\). Each constant term goes in the third column with its sign.

Expand along the first row
\[= 3\begin{vmatrix} 1 & -4 \\ -1 & -2 \end{vmatrix} - (-2)\begin{vmatrix} 1 & -4 \\ 2 & -2 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[- 2\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: the signs in the first row alternate \(+, -, +\). The middle entry is \(-2\), so its term is \(-(-2) = +2\) times its minor.

Conclusion
Thus, the given lines are concurrent.
Why: the determinant is zero and no two of the lines are parallel (slopes \(\frac{3}{2}\), \(-1\), \(2\) are all different), so Theorem 3 applies.

Find the point of concurrency
As we know that the point of intersection of any two lines is the point of concurrency. From \(x + y - 4 = 0\) and \(2x - y - 2 = 0\), we have
\[3x - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 2\]
Put \(x = 2\) in \(x + y - 4 = 0\), we have
\[2 + y - 4 = 0 \Rightarrow y = 2\]
So, \((2, 2)\) is the point of concurrency.
Why: adding the two equations cancels \(y\) (one has \(+y\), the other \(-y\)), which is the quickest elimination.

Check:
Put \((2, 2)\) in all three lines:
\[3(2) - 2(2) - 2 = 0\]
\[2 + 2 - 4 = 0\]
\[2(2) - 2 - 2 = 0\]
All three are satisfied, so the point is on every line.
blocks.answer: The determinant is \(0\), so the lines are concurrent; the point of concurrency is \((2, 2)\).

blocks.title: Challenge!
blocks.text: If the lines \(2x \quad 3y + 5 = 0\), \(3x + 4y - 1 = 0\) and \(kx - 7y + 6 = 0\) are concurrent, then find the value of \(k\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The first line of the Challenge is printed as \(2x \quad 3y + 5 = 0\): the sign between \(2x\) and \(3y\) is missing. It should be \(2x - 3y + 5 = 0\). With the minus sign, \(2x - 3y + 5 = 0\) and \(3x + 4y - 1 = 0\) meet at \((-1, 1)\) and the Challenge works out neatly. (With a plus sign the lines would meet at \((23, -17)\) and \(k = -\frac{125}{23}\), which is clearly not what the book intends.)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Try the Challenge yourself before reading this. Using Theorem 3:
\[\begin{vmatrix} 2 & -3 & 5 \\ 3 & 4 & -1 \\ k & -7 & 6 \end{vmatrix} = 0\]
\[2(24 - 7) + 3(18 + k) + 5(-21 - 4k) = 0\]
\[34 + 54 + 3k - 105 - 20k = 0\]
\[-17 - 17k = 0 \Rightarrow k = -1\]
Check: the first two lines meet at \((-1, 1)\), and \((-1)(-1) - 7(1) + 6 = 0\).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text:
Two ways to test concurrency:
1. Determinant method (Theorem 3): one calculation, and it is the method the book expects when you are asked to 'check' or 'find \(k\)'.
2. Point method: solve two of the lines, then substitute the point in the third.
When you must also give the point of concurrency, you need the point method anyway; use it as a check on the determinant.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Concurrent lines pass through one common point (the point of concurrency).
2. Theorem 3: three non-parallel lines \(a_ix + b_iy + c_i = 0\) are concurrent iff the determinant of their coefficients is zero.
3. The determinant equation is the third line evaluated at the meeting point of the first two, multiplied by \(a_1b_2 - a_2b_1\).
4. The point of concurrency is found by solving any two of the lines.
5. To find an unknown \(k\) for concurrency, set the determinant equal to zero and solve for \(k\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing the lines in the form \(ax + by = c\) and putting \(c\) in the determinant: the theorem uses \(ax + by + c = 0\), so a constant moved to the right changes sign.
2. Forgetting the minus sign on the middle term when expanding along a row.
3. Calling three parallel lines concurrent because the determinant is zero: the theorem needs non-parallel lines.
4. Stopping after 'determinant \(= 0\)' when the question also asks for the point of concurrency.
